I only feel safe in a very limited number of places

The event happened because of the way I acted
I will never be able to feel normal emotions again

vignette:
Amir had always found a certain elegant logic in code, a predictable order that governed the world inside his monitor. For thirty years as a software engineer, he had built systems on that foundation of certainty. But for the last eighteen months, since the night he was assaulted, that certainty had vanished from his life, replaced by a chaotic and threatening static he couldn't debug. He was walking home late from the office through a quiet, tree-lined street when a car with a dashboard light pulled him over. The man was large, wore a security-style jacket, and spoke with an authority that pinned Amir in place. The assault that followed was brutal and bewildering. What he remembers most vividly is lying on the pavement afterward, hearing the distant wail of an ambulance siren growing closer, then fading away down another street, leaving him utterly alone.

The world that came after was a landscape of hidden threats. Amir found he was constantly scanning his surroundings, his body locked in a state of high alert that made the open-plan office feel like a tactical field. He would react to the slightest unexpected noise as if it were a direct attack, his heart hammering in his chest. This pervasive sense of danger fed a set of dark, looping conclusions he had reached about himself and the world. He was certain that the assault had happened because of the way he acted—too compliant, too weak—and that this flaw made him permanently vulnerable. This constant feeling of being unsafe cemented his belief that what happened was not just a tragedy, but a profound injustice that had broken something fundamental within him. He was sure he would never be able to feel normal emotions again.

These convictions, in turn, dictated the rigid set of rules he now lived by. Believing himself to be at fault and that authority figures were either malicious or useless, he began to meticulously avoid any man in uniform. Seeing a police car would cause him to immediately change direction, his breath catching in his throat. This rigid avoidance extended to his work life; he could no longer tolerate being alone with male colleagues, making one-on-one meetings a source of intense dread and forcing him to communicate almost exclusively over email. Because he felt safe only in his apartment, the route between his front door and his office cubicle became the entirety of his world. He stopped going to the grocery store, ordering everything online, and has not walked down the street where the attack occurred since that night. In effect, his safety-seeking behaviours had drawn a map of the trauma onto his city, where every street he could no longer walk down and every uniform he had to avoid became a fresh reminder of his vulnerability.

This shrinking of his world only intensified his fear. By confining himself to his self-defined safe zone, everything outside it became magnified in its potential for danger, reinforcing the need to scan constantly for threats whenever he was forced to leave. The very strategies he used to feel safe made the world feel more dangerous. The sight of an ambulance, once a symbol of help, now became a potent trigger, the sound of its siren a direct echo of his abandonment. Hearing one from his apartment window would send a jolt of panic through him, validating his decision not to go out and further narrowing the map of his life.

The isolation born from his avoidance served as daily proof of his own narrative of being permanently damaged. Each project meeting he skipped because it involved being in a room with men he didn't know well confirmed his self-blame and the crushing belief that he was incapable of normal interaction. His world, once rich with colleagues and acquaintances, had contracted to the dimensions of his screen. It was a recent performance review, where his manager gently noted his increasing isolation and lack of collaboration, that finally prompted him to seek help. Amir confessed that he no longer knew how to exist outside his apartment without the constant, exhausting hum of fear. He came to therapy not with anger, but with a quiet, desperate question: was it possible to ever feel safe enough to feel like himself again?
